variants.name: Class template on a state tag (move-based)
variants.idiom_name: class template parameterized by a state tag, rvalue-qualified transitions
variants.implementation_notes: Everything is hand-written: empty tag structs (or an enum) name the states, one class template carries the state as a parameter, and each transition is an rvalue-qualified ('&&') member that constructs the next instantiation and destroys the previous value. Deleted copy operations, private constructors, a friend factory and static_asserts keep the protocol closed - FluentC++ lists exactly this checklist, which is why wrapper libraries such as ProtEnc and Coconut exist. The standard library provides nothing, but the encoding still costs nothing at run time, and the per-state-class form remains the fallback when states carry different data or the toolchain predates C++11.
pitfalls: Without the && qualifier (or an explicit std::move of the payload) the source state stays usable, so the transition looks like a normal member call and the guarantee is gone.
static_asserts or enable_if constraints must be repeated in every transition; one forgotten check leaves a hole in the protocol that the compiler will happily accept.

Deleting both copy and move changes the design: move-based transitions need the move constructor, while the value-passing form (transitions only on prvalues) deletes both and passes references instead.

variants.name: One class per state with friend transitions
variants.idiom_name: one class per state, private constructors and friend transitions
variants.implementation_notes: Each state is its own class (HttpBuilderWithoutHeader, HttpBuilderWithBody, ...) with a private constructor and transitions declared as friends, so only the state's own operations exist on its type; a transition returns the next state class, converting or moving the payload. This avoids template diagnostics and works in C++03, at the cost of duplicated members and conversion boilerplate that grows with every state.
pitfalls: Each conversion between state classes duplicates or moves the payload; a missing std::move copies it on every transition.
Friend declarations and duplicated accessors are easy to get wrong: a leaked public constructor lets callers enter a state directly.
